order: If someone you met three days ago says you're their favourite person in the whole world... don't say it back. Especially if she doesn't blink.
If your phone is off... and it still lights up: "I can see your light's still on"... don't look out the window.
And if you look down at midnight... and someone at your blue front door is smiling up, two words chalked at their feet...
When I was twelve, my best friend handed me seven rules on a card. His mom's purple handwriting. At the top, one name, scribbled out in blue pen.

That week, a new girl decided I'd be her best friend. Only hers. By Saturday midnight, she was on our doormat, my sister was reading a name under the landing light... and I was halfway down the stairs to let her in.
Danny had been my best friend since we were seven. Now he ate lunch with Kofi and Sam. Chewed blue pen behind his ear.
At seven, on the swings, I made up a song for him.
Me and you, and you and me, stick like glue, and you will see. Everywhere you go, I'm near. Only me. I'm here, I'm here.
I made it up. Nobody else knows it.
Danny's wrist was bare. The green-and-gold bracelet I wove him in third grade... gone.
Monday, Mom held up my grey hoodie. Sleeves white to the elbow.
Anything you want to tell me?
She looked a beat too long.
Behind our school: an old hopscotch. All new paint, except the top square. Faded red.
Hop it alone at sunset. Chalk a name, and under it, only me. That person will never leave you.
Nobody was cruel enough to try it.
In the square, someone had chalked a little girl. Two braids. A smile that didn't stop.
That day, a new girl sat behind me. Freckles. Gap-tooth grin. Braids tied with faded red ribbons.
By Tuesday, she was waiting at my locker. She knew my favourite crisps.
Somebody waiting for me, for once.
Wednesday, at my shoulder... she didn't blink.
You're my favourite person in the whole world.
Then Danny crossed the hall, first time in weeks, with the card.
My mom wrote these. For when someone holds on too tight. They helped.
You don't have to answer after goodnight. Phone off. Sleep.
Every ping, one note of my song. Twelve messages. Thirty. Forty-seven.
I kept rule one. Phone off.
The dark screen lit up anyway.
I can see your light's still on.
Under the streetlight, Evie smiled up. At her feet, in big curly chalk...
I switched off my light. Below me, our porch light clicked on. Evie lay down flat, like a chalk drawing... and slid away.
Thursday morning, our path was wet and clean.
Bucket by the door. Mom on the phone, knuckles red.
I know. I'll talk to him. Thank you for telling me.
On our wet step: one white sneaker print. Pointing in.
Forty-seven messages, in one night. Before rule two, one word in the comments.
If someone did that for you... would you feel Special, or Trapped?
A gift is not a bill. If a present makes you feel you owe someone, give it back.
Inside my locked locker: a woven bracelet. Green and gold. Chalk dust on it.
Suddenly Evie was one inch from my shoulder. Not touching. Never touching.
I made it myself. For you. Only me?
She didn't. I did. It was Danny's bracelet.
So Danny gave it away. And I'd only ever messaged him a normal amount.
I kept it. Heavy as a stone.
That night, only me was halfway up our path. Evie on it, smiling up.
Her smile was a white chalk line now. Just past the corners.
Your password is yours. Your location is for your parents only.
At lunch, Evie slid her phone across the table.
Best friends share passwords. Don't you trust me?
On my map, a white dot joined my blue one.
Her dot got everywhere first. The bus stop. The shop. Danny's street.
Two a.m. Her dot was on our house.
Just one white chalk fingerprint... on the inside of my window.
Outside, only me had reached the foot of our step.
Friday. Mrs. Rahman, the counsellor, at her open door.
Just checking in, Adam. My door's open.
On my phone, mute icons. By Mom. By my sister, Lina. By Danny.
If someone keeps turning up where you are, tell a grown-up. Never go alone to sort it out.
Mom's car. Red light. Evie, on the pavement, right by my window.
At break, on the swings, she sang my song. Every word perfect.
At sunset, I went to sort it out. Alone. Her white prints led to the square.
It was covered in chalk. My handwriting. My curly M's.
A name, rubbed out: Danny. Written over it: Adam. And under that...
From the square, slowed down, came my song. In my seven-year-old voice.
I told you nobody was cruel enough to try it.
Last Sunday. I'd chalked Danny's name. I thought it hadn't worked.
The chalk slid out, flat across the playground... and stood up.
Arms spread across the gate. Never touching.
You asked for someone who'd never leave. Here I am.
Floodlight. The caretaker, squinting right at us. She was flat chalk again.
That night, only me was on our step. Under it, one empty chalk line. Waiting for a name.
A real friend is happy you have other people. Never let anyone pull you away from your family.
Behind Mom, outside the dark window, Evie's lips moved. My phone buzzed with every word.
Your mom's always on the phone about you. She thinks something's wrong with you.
Your sister's a baby. Only I get you.
Anything you want to tell me?
I pulled my phone into my lap.
Lina held out a drawing of us. I snapped at her and went upstairs.
I typed it. And I heard myself.
I threw Danny's card on the landing.
Only me moved onto our doorstep. Right against our green front door.
There's a girl at our door. She's smiling up at your window.
Evie's neck was bending. Up... and up... toward my window. Her chalk smile almost touched her ears.
If someone says their feelings are your fault, they're not. You're allowed to leave.
From the landing, I heard our letterbox lift.
Chalk-white fingers slid through. Far too long. Creeping across the hall floor, writing...
Through the slot, a smile, ear to ear. Humming my song. Slow. Flat.
If you leave, it's your fault. I'll stand here forever.
A chalk stub dropped through, rolling to the bottom stair.
Write your name. Under only me.
My feet moved. One step down. Two. Halfway.
Behind me, the landing light clicked on.
Lina, under the bare bulb, held up Danny's card. Light showed through the scribble.
The rules weren't for me. Danny's mom wrote them to protect Danny.
Don't keep it secret. Tell a grown-up. Save the messages. If they don't listen, tell another. Keep telling.
I stepped over the chalk. I didn't go to the door.
The kitchen light was already on. Mom, still dressed. Bucket by the door. Red knuckles.
I told her everything. The square. The bracelet. My password. Evie.
Behind me, the letterbox rattled. Chalk fingers wrote M... E... toward the kitchen.
The letters crept across the tiles... and stopped at her chair.
She'd said that on the phone every morning. To Danny's mom.
It never rained. Every dawn, Mom had scrubbed my handwriting off our path. She'd called Mrs. Rahman. She'd sat up every night, listening. And she'd kept asking, until I let her in.
Mom saved every message from Evie.
Each one a note of my song.
Then I scrolled to Danny. My thread. And stopped.
The same words. Word for word. Sent by me.
Forty-seven. In one night. A normal amount.
That blue front door was Danny's.
Sunday. Midnight. Chalk-white sleeves. Smiling up at his dark window, two words at my feet.
Danny didn't go down. He woke his mom.
Danny was right to say no. And you're not bad.
She opened our front door and stood beside me.
Evie was on our doormat, smiling ear to ear.
Mom looked right at her. Evie came no closer.
No. I'm not your only. And Danny was never mine.
I hope you find lots of people.
Only me. I'm here, I'm he-
Her colour drained to chalk-white, and the wind carried her off like dust.
At dawn, we scrubbed the path together. The hall floor, I did myself.
Lina sang new words to my old tune.
Me and you, and others too, friends for me and friends for you. Go wherever, near or far. I'll still care, wherever you are.
Monday, I told Mrs. Rahman too.
I think I'm the one who couldn't let go.
That was brave. Caring isn't owning. We'll work on it together.
With Mom beside me, I sent Danny one message.
Sorry. I'll give you space. You don't have to answer.
No reply. I didn't send another. Maybe he'd never answer. That had to be okay.
The bracelet in my drawer was chalk dust. The caretaker painted over the Keeping Square.
Weeks later, Danny stopped at my table. Kofi and Sam too.
Can we sit here? All of us?
Danny slid over a shoebox. Every gift I'd given him. On top, the real bracelet.
Then the card. The scribble... in his chewed blue pen.
I crossed it out. You were still my friend. I just needed room.
He's not my only friend. He's one of my best.
Last week, Danny didn't answer all day. My fingertips went white. That old pull.
Next morning, one chalk word on my path.
I scrubbed it off, the way Mom did.
He picked up on the first ring.
Okay. Breathe. You can turn a light on now.
None of this happened. No Keeping Square, no Evie, no chalk.
The monster is made up. The warning signs are real.
Too much, too fast. Nonstop messages. Gifts that make you feel you owe them.
Wanting you all to themselves. Turning up uninvited. Putting down your family and friends.
Your passwords are yours. Your location is for your parents.
"It's your fault" is never true. You can say no, not answer, block and report. Saying no isn't cruel.
Don't keep it secret. Tell a grown-up. Save the messages. Keep telling.
Can't stop checking on someone? That's holding on, not caring. Tell a grown-up. Asking for help is brave.
You can't make anyone like you. And nobody can make you owe them.
Those forty-seven messages were mine first. To Danny.
If you said Special, that's what I thought I gave him. If you said Trapped, that's what he felt.
Reply to your comment with the word that fixes both: Space.
And subscribe. On Night Policy, you can leave whenever you want. That's how you know we're real friends.
Sleep well. And if anyone ever promises they'll never let you go...
...ask them what happens when you say no.
